text: Imagine Tiny’s big sibling, a real language model. It gets one hard question right. Pure luck.
So we push that lucky answer up. Hard. Again, and again.
Then we ask it two plus two. Seven?! Five plus one... seven! Nine plus nine... seven!
One lucky answer, pushed too far, and the whole model went wrong.
Okay, that’s terrifying. How do we stop it?
GRPO has two safety brakes. By the end of this video, you’ll know exactly when each one kicks in.
Brakes. Like on a bike?
Pretty much. One stops a single batch from overreacting. The other keeps the model close to home.
Clipping and the KL leash. Episode two.
First, why would one batch move the model too far?
Writing answers is the slowest, most expensive part. So it’s tempting to reuse them.
Like, sample once, then learn from the same answers a few times?
Exactly. Several small steps on the same batch. In the code, the setting is called num iterations.
But after the first step, the model has already changed. Push the same lucky answer four times, and slightly more likely becomes the only thing it says.
So we need a way to measure how far an answer has moved. That’s the ratio.
It’s the answer’s chance now, divided by its chance when it was sampled.
So if it was ten percent, and now it’s twelve percent...
The ratio is one point two. Twenty percent more likely than when we sampled it.
And on the very first step, the ratio is always exactly one, because nothing has moved yet.
Now, clipping. Picture a fence around one, from zero point eight to one point two.
That’s twenty percent either way, the usual setting. In papers, that twenty percent is called epsilon.
Okay, Tiny’s answer was good, so we push it up. Push... push again...
And once it’s twenty percent more likely than when it was sampled, the rule says: that’s enough for now. Stop pushing.
Same on the other side. A bad answer gets pushed down until it’s twenty percent less likely. Then it stops too.
Here’s a tricky one. A bad answer, with a negative advantage, somehow became more likely. Its ratio is one point five, way outside the fence.
Does clipping stop the update?
Pause, and have a guess.
A! It’s outside the fence, so the brake kicks in. Stop!
That’s the trap. It’s B. Clipping only stops you going too far in the direction you wanted.
This answer went the wrong way, so the rule keeps pushing it back down. Clipping never blocks a fix.
In the Tiny Adder code, the whole rule is a few lines.
If the answer was good, and it’s already more than twenty percent up: clipped.
If it was bad, and it’s already more than twenty percent down: clipped.
And anything else still gets nudged. Including our wrong-way answer!
Exactly. Clipped just means: this answer stops adding to the step.
So does the brake help Tiny? Here’s an experiment from the lesson: four steps per batch, with and without clipping.
Wait. The clipped one is slower?!
Much slower. At step fifty: about a quarter, against two thirds.
So the brake just... makes it worse?
On the toy, yes. Tiny’s answers for each sum live in separate boxes, so overshooting costs almost nothing.
A real model shares every weight across millions of situations. There, clipping is insurance. On the toy, you only see the price, never the crash.
But many tiny, safe steps can still carry the model far from where it started.
Like a puppy that wanders off, one sniff at a time.
Ha, exactly. So the second brake is a leash. We keep a frozen copy of the starting model, called the reference.
Every step, we measure how far the model has drifted from it, and subtract a penalty. That distance is the KL.
And how hard the leash pulls is called beta.
On Tiny, here’s the reward after two hundred steps, for three leash strengths.
No leash: eighty-six percent.
A loose leash: sixty-two.
And a tight one, beta zero point five: six percent. The leash pulls back as hard as the reward pushes, and Tiny stays stuck, guessing.
Two brakes, side by side.
Clipping stops one batch overreacting, and it only matters when you take several steps per batch.
The leash stops slow drift, over the whole run.
So which one do people actually use?
Both, loosely. With right-or-wrong maths rewards, the model is supposed to change a lot, so many recipes switch the leash off. The default is now beta zero.
Quick recap.
The ratio says how far an answer has moved since it was sampled.
Clipping stops pushing once it has moved enough, but never blocks a fix.
And the leash keeps the model from wandering too far from home.
Now we’ve got every piece. But Tiny’s whole brain is a table of just nineteen hundred numbers.
Hang on. So all of this has only ever run on a toy?
What happens on a real model? With half a billion numbers? Can we even afford that?
We can. Next episode, we set up the real thing, on a free GPU.
